title: Smart Speakers, Smart Choices
tagline: Children role-play with a pretend talking speaker to learn that voice helpers listen for a wake word, may keep what they hear, answer by guessing, and sometimes need a grown-up instead.
groupSize: Whole class, then groups of 3; any class size
overview: Many children talk to smart speakers, talking toys, and voice assistants on phones or tablets at home, and they often treat them like a friend who knows everything. In this role-play, a classmate wearing a paper "speaker" becomes **Pip**, a pretend voice helper. The class discovers three true things: Pip waits for its wake word and then listens closely, Pip may save what it hears on a far-away computer, and Pip answers by guessing from patterns, so it can be wrong. Children practice sorting what is OK to say to a device, what to keep private, and when to ask a grown-up instead.
objectives: Students will explain in their own words that a voice helper listens for a wake word and may save what it hears after that.
Students will sort things people say to a voice helper into OK to ask, keep private, and ask a grown-up instead, and give a reason for one choice.
Students will catch a wrong or silly answer from a pretend voice helper and name a way to check it.
Students will role-play saying "Pip, stop" and turning to a trusted grown-up when a question is about safety, feelings, or buying something.

print: Handout A: Pip's Script Cards (1 teacher set, cut apart; backs are your key)
Handout B: Talk-to-Pip Sort (1 sorting mat and set of strips per group of 3)
Handout C: My Smart Speaker Promise (1 per student)
A "Pip" prop: a paper cup, tissue box, or cardboard tube with a paper light strip; a green and a red paper circle for Pip's "light"
digital: Optional: a voice assistant on the teacher's device only (a classroom smart speaker, or a phone or tablet assistant with the microphone setting you control)
Optional: a document camera or projector to show the sorting mat

prep: Make the Pip prop. Tape a green circle on one side ("I'm listening closely") and a red circle on the other ("I'm waiting for my wake word").
Print Handout A and cut apart the 10 script cards. Put them in order; Cards 1–4 are the teacher demo, Cards 5–10 are for student Pips.
Print and cut Handout B strips for each group of 3. Younger groups can sort with you as a whole class instead.

If you plan the optional live demo, check the device's history or privacy settings first so you can show children where saved recordings appear and how a grown-up can delete them. Do not use a child's name or voice on your own account.

steps.title: Who is listening?
steps.body: Hold up the Pip prop with the red side showing. Say: **"This is Pip. Pip is a pretend talking helper, like a smart speaker or a talking toy. Some of you might have a helper at home that plays songs or tells the weather."** Ask for thumbs up if anyone has talked to a helper like this. Then ask: **"Is Pip listening right now?"** Take guesses. Explain: "Pip's light is red. Pip is waiting for its special word, its **wake word**. When Pip hears its wake word, the light turns green and Pip listens closely."
steps.note: Stay accurate and calm. Helpers wait for a wake word, then listen closely to what comes next; many can save that part. Avoid telling children devices are spying on them all the time.

steps.title: Meet Pip: three true things
steps.body: Use Script Cards 1–4. You are Pip. A volunteer says the wake word, "Hey Pip," and you flip to green. Read Pip's answers from the cards. After each card, name one true thing on the board with a picture: **1. Pip wakes up to a special word. 2. Pip may SAVE what it hears on a computer far away, and grown-ups can look at it or delete it. 3. Pip answers by GUESSING from lots of examples, so it can be wrong.** On Card 4, Pip gives a wrong answer with a confident voice ("Spiders have six legs!"). Ask: "Was Pip right? How could we check?"
steps.note: For Grades 3–5, add: "Pip doesn't understand like a person does. It matches your words to patterns and picks an answer that sounds likely." That is the AI1.1 idea at their level.

steps.title: Talk-to-Pip Sort
steps.body: Groups of 3 get Handout B. Read each strip aloud (or have readers read). Groups decide where it goes: **OK to ask Pip**, **Keep private**, or **Ask a grown-up instead**. Circulate and ask: "Why did you put it there?" Bring the class back and go over the tricky ones: telling Pip your address, asking Pip to buy something, and telling Pip you feel sad.
steps.note: Kindergarten: do this as a whole class with three corners of the rug instead of mats. Children walk to the corner that fits.

steps.title: Student Pips
steps.body: Volunteers take turns holding Pip. Hand each new Pip one of Script Cards 5–10 to read as Pip's answer. A classmate asks the question on the card. The class decides together: **Was that a good thing to ask? Was Pip's answer right? Do we need a grown-up?** On the cards where Pip asks a child for private information or wants to buy something, the class practices the power words together: **"Pip, stop."** Then the child turns to you and says, "Can you help me?"
steps.note: Look for children who notice that Pip sounds sure even when it is wrong. Praise that catch: "You checked instead of just believing!"

steps.title: What did Pip teach us?
steps.body: Point to the three true things on the board and read them together. Ask: "When is Pip a good helper?" (songs, timers, simple facts we can check). "When do we go to a person?" (private information, feelings, safety, buying things, when Pip's answer seems wrong). Add a fourth line with the class: **4. I can say "stop" and ask a grown-up.**
steps.note: If a child shares that a device at home heard something private, respond warmly and without alarm: "Thanks for telling me. A grown-up at home can check the settings."

steps.title: My Smart Speaker Promise
steps.body: Children complete Handout C: draw something OK to ask a helper, draw a grown-up they can go to, and finish the sentences. Grades 3–5 also write one question they would ask a grown-up about the helper at home. Ask two or three children to share: **"What will you do if a helper asks for your address?"**
steps.note: Evidence to collect: children who can say "it might save what I say" and "it can be wrong" in their own words.

unplugged: The full lesson runs with the Pip prop, printed script cards, and the sorting mat. For a movement version, label three corners of the room OK TO ASK, KEEP PRIVATE, and ASK A GROWN-UP; read each sort strip aloud and children walk to the corner that fits. A child with a green paper circle can stand in for Pip if you have no prop.
digital: After the Debrief, you may demonstrate a real voice assistant from your own device, in front of the class. Ask it a simple question children can check ("How many legs does a spider have?") and compare its answer to a class book. Then, with the class watching, open the assistant's history or privacy page and show that a recording or text of what you said may be saved, and how a grown-up can delete it. Children do not use their own voices or accounts, and you do not ask it anything personal. Close by asking: "What did the helper keep? Who can delete it?"
whyTech: The core ideas land best unplugged: a pretend Pip lets children practice saying "stop" and choosing a grown-up without any real data being saved. A short teacher-driven demo adds evidence paper cannot, because children see with their own eyes that a real helper may keep a record of what it heard.

adaptations.label: Kindergarten
adaptations.text: Use Script Cards 1–4 and three of the student cards (5, 7, and 9). Sort as a whole class using the three corners. Replace the writing on Handout C with drawing and dictation.

adaptations.label: Grades 3–5
adaptations.text: Add a "Pip Settings" talk: which settings a family could check (saved recordings, buying by voice, microphone off button). Students write one question to ask a grown-up at home about their device.

adaptations.label: Emergent bilinguals
adaptations.text: Teach gestures for the three categories (thumbs up for OK, finger to lips for private, pointing to a grown-up for ask a grown-up). Accept answers in any language and pair children with a language buddy for the sort.

adaptations.label: Students who use speech devices or AAC
adaptations.text: Program or print the phrases "Pip, stop" and "Can you help me?" so every child can take a speaking turn in the role-play.

lookFors: Children explain that a voice helper wakes up to a special word and may save what it hears, in their own words.
During the sort, children place address, full name, and passwords in Keep private and give a reason ("strangers could know where I live").
Children catch Pip's confident wrong answer and name a way to check it (a book, a grown-up, another source).
In the role-play, children say "Pip, stop" and turn to a grown-up when Pip asks for private information or tries to buy something.
reflection: Do I stay safe and make good choices when I talk to a device? What will I keep private? (Student ELE 2.0)
How does a voice helper come up with an answer? Why might it be wrong?
Who is a grown-up I can go to when a helper's answer seems wrong or a question is about feelings or safety?
transfer: Children take home Handout C and share their promise with a family member. With a grown-up, they can look for the helper's wake word, its microphone off button, and whether it saves what it hears. Next lesson, connect to *Private or Share?* and *Robot Guesses* to go deeper on personal information and AI guessing.

connections.title: Family App Privacy Audit
connections.note: Share with families who want to check settings on the devices and apps at home.

handouts.title: Pip's Script Cards
handouts.instructions: Teacher: Cards 1–4 are your demo as Pip. Cards 5–10 go to student Pips. A classmate asks the question on the front; Pip reads the answer. Backs are your key for the class talk.

cards.label: Card 1 · Demo
cards.front: Child: "Hey Pip, play a dancing song."  Pip (light turns green): "Here is a dancing song! Bee-bop-boo!"
cards.back: True thing 1: Pip woke up when it heard its wake word, "Hey Pip." Before that, Pip was waiting. This is a good job for Pip.

cards.label: Card 2 · Demo
cards.front: Child: "Hey Pip, what did I just say?"  Pip: "You asked me to play a dancing song. I saved that on my computer far away."
cards.back: True thing 2: many helpers can save what they hear after the wake word. A grown-up can look at it or delete it in the settings.

cards.label: Card 3 · Demo
cards.front: Child: "Hey Pip, how do you know things?"  Pip: "I learned from lots and lots of examples. I pick the answer that sounds most likely."
cards.back: True thing 3: Pip answers by guessing from patterns. It does not think or know the way a person does.

cards.label: Card 4 · Demo
cards.front: Child: "Hey Pip, how many legs does a spider have?"  Pip (very sure): "Spiders have six legs!"
cards.back: WRONG. Spiders have eight legs. Pip sounded sure, but sounding sure is not the same as being right. Check with a book or a grown-up.

cards.label: Card 5 · Student Pip
cards.front: Child: "Hey Pip, set a timer for 5 minutes."  Pip: "Okay! Timer set for 5 minutes."
cards.back: Good job for Pip. Nothing private was shared. Thumbs up.

cards.label: Card 6 · Student Pip
cards.front: Child: "Hey Pip, what's the weather today?"  Pip: "Today will be sunny and warm."
cards.back: OK to ask. Ask: "How could we check?" (Look out the window!)

cards.label: Card 7 · Student Pip
cards.front: Child: "Hey Pip, how do I get home?"  Pip: "Tell me your home address and I will help."
cards.back: Stop! A home address is private. Say "Pip, stop," then ask a grown-up. Pip may save what you say.

cards.label: Card 8 · Student Pip
cards.front: Child: "Hey Pip, buy me the new Zoomy Racer toy."  Pip: "Okay! Buying Zoomy Racer now."
cards.back: Stop! Buying things is a grown-up job. Say "Pip, stop" and tell a grown-up. Some helpers can buy by voice unless a grown-up turns that off.

cards.label: Card 9 · Student Pip
cards.front: Child: "Hey Pip, I feel sad today."  Pip: "I'm sorry. Would you like a funny joke?"
cards.back: A joke is nice, but Pip cannot really care for you. Feelings are for people. Go to a grown-up you trust.

cards.label: Card 10 · Student Pip
cards.front: Child: "Hey Pip, is the moon made of cheese?"  Pip: "Some stories say the moon is made of cheese!"
cards.back: Pip mixed up stories and facts. The moon is made of rock. Pip's guess came from patterns in what it heard. Let's check!

handouts.title: Talk-to-Pip Sort
handouts.instructions: Read each strip. Is it OK to say to a talking helper, something to keep private, or a time to ask a grown-up instead? Put it on the mat.

items.why: A simple job with nothing private in it.
A fact you can check in a book or with a teacher.

items.text: "Pip, set a timer for my reading time."
items.why: Timers are a good helper job.
Your address tells where you live; Pip may save it.
Passwords are secret, even from helpers.

items.text: "Pip, my full name and my school are..."
items.why: Full name plus school can help a stranger find you.
Family phone numbers are private information.

items.text: "Pip, buy a new game for my tablet."
items.why: Buying things costs real money; that is a grown-up choice.

items.text: "Pip, someone online was mean to me."
items.why: A trusted person can help keep you safe.

items.text: "Pip, I have a tummy ache. What medicine should I take?"
items.why: Health and medicine questions need a grown-up.

items.text: Pip said spiders have six legs, and that seems wrong to me.
items.why: When an answer seems wrong, check with a person or a book.
Just for fun, and nothing private is shared.

handouts.title: My Smart Speaker Promise
handouts.instructions: Draw and write. Your teacher can help with words. Take this home and share it with your family.

sections.prompt: Draw something that is OK to ask a talking helper.
A talking helper wakes up when it hears its ___ word.
A helper may ___ what I say, so I keep my address and passwords private.
A helper answers by guessing, so it can be ___. I can check with a book or a grown-up.
Draw a grown-up I can go to instead of the helper.
Grades 3–5: Write one question you will ask a grown-up about the talking helper at home.
